one_liner: Rust AV1 encoder with dav1d-derived SIMD asm and a C API; its 'fastest' claim is unsupported: slower than libaom at equal quality.
what_it_does: An AV1 encoder shipped as a Rust crate, a rav1e CLI (y4m in, IVF out) and a C library built with cargo-c. The Rust API builds a Config/EncoderConfig, creates a Context, and pushes frames with send_frame and pulls packets with receive_packet. The C API mirrors that (rav1e_config_default, rav1e_config_parse key/value strings, rav1e_context_new, rav1e_send_frame, rav1e_receive_packet, plus two-pass rate-control calls). It covers 8/10/12-bit 4:2:0, 4:2:2 and 4:4:4, constant-quantizer and single- or two-pass bitrate modes, and still-picture mode. It is not an API drop-in for libaom's aom_codec_* interface, but its output is a standard AV1 bitstream that any compliant decoder (dav1d, libaom) can play.
how_it_is_fast: Speed comes mainly from presets 0-10 that prune rate-distortion search. The default, speed 6, drops RDO transform-type decision, uses the reduced transform set, disables full-search motion estimation and cuts temporal-RDO lookahead to 20 frames. Speed 7+ uses simple prediction modes, a single reference and fast deblocking; speed 8 turns off loop restoration; speeds 9-10 restrict partitions to 16x16-32x32 and then 32x32 only, with fast scene detection and no SATD subpel. Distortion is measured in the transform domain by default. The hot kernels are hand-written NASM imported from dav1d (motion compensation, inverse transforms, intra prediction, CDEF, loop filter, loop restoration, film grain; VideoLAN/Two Orioles headers), plus rav1e's own SAD, SATD, motion-search and CDEF-distortion asm, in SSE2 through AVX-512 (Ice Lake) versions picked at runtime by CPUID, and NEON on aarch64. Threads come from a rayon pool working across tiles; there is no frame-parallel encoding.
when_to_use: Rust codebases that need an AV1 or AVIF encoder without linking libaom: ravif, its largest crates.io dependent (20.7M downloads), builds on it, and rav1e itself has 49.7M downloads.

Still-image AVIF encoding (still_picture mode), where per-frame encode speed matters less than a permissively licensed (BSD-2-Clause plus the AOM patent license) encoder written mostly in a memory-safe language.

Chunked, many-process pipelines (Av1an style), where a fast preset that gives up compression is acceptable. In the independent 2020 Av1an run, speed 6 finished about 1.7x faster than aomenc cpu-used 6 but needed about 16% more bitrate for the same VMAF (derived from page data).
C or C++ applications that want a small encoder API with string key/value configuration (rav1e_config_parse) and a pkg-config package.
when_not_to_use: When encode time at a given quality matters, which is the actual comparison with libaom. The maintainers' own issue #2759 (2021, still open) says speed 6 trails aomenc cpu-used 6 by about 30% BD-rate while also being slower single-tile, and that matching aomenc needs speed 0 at about 2700% more time. In the 2020 Av1an run, aomenc cpu-used 6 reached slightly better VMAF BD-rate (-1.571%) than rav1e speed 0 in 87.3% less time.

Single-stream encodes on many cores with default settings: a 1080p encode uses one tile unless you pass --tiles or tile_cols/tile_rows, and frame-parallel encoding is missing (doc/QUALITY_&_SPEED_FEATURES.md). Parallel-GOP encoding exists only behind the unstable channel API, and issue #1831 ('Improve the multithread support') has been open since 2019.

Low-latency or bitrate-capped live encoding through the C API: open issue #3416 reports packets far above a 200 kb/s target, 13 frames of delay with rdo_lookahead_frames=5, and no latency change from tiles or threads. It has no maintainer reply.

When you need the 'safest' claim to hold in practice: much of the speed lives in hand-written assembly, issue #3469 (May 2026) asks for a private channel to report API soundness issues and has no public answer, and issue #3392 reports an illegal-instruction crash on Apple M1 with 0.7.1.
Monochrome input (not supported, per the README) or development that expects regular releases: crates.io is still at 0.8.1 (2025-06-16), and the last weekly pre-release is p20250902.

integration.form: crate (Rust library plus rav1e CLI); C static/shared library with header and pkg-config via cargo-c
integration.dependencies: NASM 2.14.02+ on x86_64 for the default asm feature (gas or clang assembler on aarch64); Rust crates including maybe-rayon, av-scenechange, v_frame, bitstream-io, av1-grain; cargo-c to build the C API
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE2 baseline; SSSE3, SSE4.1, AVX2, AVX-512 and AVX-512 ICL asm chosen at runtime, RAV1E_CPU_TARGET overrides), aarch64 NEON, pure-Rust fallback elsewhere, wasm feature; no Windows arm64 release binaries (#3425), no RISC-V asm (#3402)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented for concurrent calls on one Context. Internally it uses a rayon thread pool (threads=0 means all logical CPUs) shared by tile encoding and lookahead; the CLI help warns that more tiles may be needed to use the threads.

gotchas: The published 0.8.0 and 0.8.1 crates depend on av-scenechange with default features off and no 'asm' feature (checked on crates.io), so scene-change detection runs without its assembly. Commit b7bf390 (2025-09-21) says this was 'accidentally disabled' during the migration to that crate and re-enables it, but no release carries the fix yet; the slowdown has not been measured.
The default is speed 6, not 0. The C API documentation lists rdo_lookahead_frames as default 40, but the speed-6 preset sets 20, so read the effective settings rather than the doc comment.

Building with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' or x86-64-v3 is 11-13% faster per the README, but the binary then faults on CPUs that lack AVX2, BMI1/2, FMA, LZCNT or POPCNT. RAV1E_CPU_TARGET=rust disables all asm at runtime, which is useful for bisecting asm bugs.
The README's 'weekly pre-release every Tuesday' is stale: master has commits through 2026-08-31, but the newest pre-release (p20250902) and crate (0.8.1) date from 2025.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against SVT-AV1, pick rav1e for a Rust-native crate, AVIF through ravif, or a small BSD-licensed C API, and pick SVT-AV1 when throughput at a given quality on many cores matters. rusty-av1-toolkit, a rav1e derivative, claims about 1.10x shorter encode time with byte-identical output in its default mode, so check it if you are tied to rav1e's bitstream. dav1d is a decoder and does not compete.
verified_claims_summary: The repository holds no speed number against libaom. Its only measured figure is an internal 11-13% gain from target-cpu builds, and benches/ has only criterion microbenchmarks of write_b, CDEF, CfL RDO, intra prediction and entropy coding at speed 10. The external evidence runs against the claim. Maintainer issue #2759 (2021) puts rav1e behind aomenc at matched presets. The independent master-of-zen 2020.08.05 Av1an run (xiph dota2 clip, 8-bit, git snapshots of each encoder, CPU model and flags unstated, chunked wall time) shows rav1e speed 6 at a mean 38.9 s against 66.9 s for aomenc cpu-used 6, but rav1e needs roughly 16% more bitrate for the same VMAF. Speed 10 is about 3x faster only with a BD-rate gap above 60% (derived from page data). Its speed lead therefore comes from doing less compression work.
status_note: Maintenance mode: the last commits (2026-08-31) are an MSRV bump and a rand update, the last functional fix dates from Sep 2025, and crates.io is still at 0.8.1 (2025-06-16). It remains widely used (49.7M crates.io downloads, mostly through ravif), BSD-2-Clause with the AOM patent license, and easy to vendor as a crate or a cargo-c C library.
